notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Black on white plates in the format 00A-A-000, with no region code and no emblem, so they say nothing about where the car was registered.

notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Plates only use letters that look the same in Latin and Cyrillic: A, E, O, J, K, M and T.

notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Temporary plates start with red letters TT followed by six digits.

notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Taxi plates use the format TA followed by six digits.

notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Diplomatic plates are on a blue background with yellow characters; the middle letter is A, C, M or E.

notes.subject: plate
notes.text: Older plates issued before 2009 are still in use; those from the mid-1990s have a blue strip on the left and a two-letter city code.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Road signs use both Latin and Cyrillic script, and some built-up-area signs come in versions with or without the Cyrillic line.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Signs follow the Vienna Convention and differ little from those of neighbouring ex-Yugoslav states.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Some information signs, such as hospital, police and dead end, have different designs in the two main administrative entities.

notes.subject: language
notes.text: No single official language; three closely related regional languages are recognised, written in Latin and Cyrillic.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Web domains end in .ba and the phone code is +387.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Largely mountainous, especially in the central and eastern parts, which are dominated by the Dinaric Alps.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: The smaller southern region has a Mediterranean climate and is also mostly mountainous; there is only a roughly 20 km Adriatic coastline.
